# Brave New Hive

> A marketing pedia for brands in the age of AI. The Hive is where the knowledge is kept. brave-new.com is where it gets used.

Full text of every entry. Published by Brave New. Every entry is dated, sourced and signed by Anne Becheru.

## 01 Principles

The handful of ideas most marketing still rests on, each with the person and the year it came from.

### The 4 Ps of marketing

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/principles/4-ps-of-marketing/
Date: 2026-09-08. Read: 10 min.

The marketing mix says a marketer's job is to set four controllable variables: product, price, place and promotion. It is a classification, not a theory, and has never been tested as one. What has been tested is the weight of each element. Across 70 French brands, product and distribution moved long-run sales at roughly ten times the elasticity of advertising and discounting [11]. Practitioners run the mix backwards: they lead promotion and leave price and place to others [15]. Own the whole list or stop calling it a mix.

## Origin

The idea has three authors and the wrong one gets the credit.

In 1948 James Culliton, in a Harvard research bulletin on manufacturers' marketing costs, described the marketing executive as a "mixer of ingredients" [2]. His colleague Neil Borden built a concept round the phrase: if the executive was a mixer of ingredients, "what he designed was a 'marketing mix'" [1, p. 4]. Borden used the idea in teaching and consulting before he wrote it up in the Journal of Advertising Research in 1964, where his "Elements of the Marketing Mix of Manufacturers" ran to twelve items: product planning, pricing, branding, channels of distribution, personal selling, advertising, promotions, packaging, display, servicing, physical handling, and fact finding and analysis [1, pp. 4 to 5]. He added, in the same breath, "I realize others might build a different list" [1, p. 4].

One of the others was E. Jerome McCarthy, whose Basic Marketing: A Managerial Approach (Richard D. Irwin, 1960) cut the mix to four groups of decisions and gave them the alliteration that made them teachable: product, place, promotion, price [3]. "Four P's" appears on twenty pages of the 1960 edition [3].

The problem McCarthy was solving was pedagogical. Borden's twelve elements were a case teacher's checklist; McCarthy needed a structure students could carry into an exam. Four boxes did that. Be precise about what kind of thing the 4 Ps are: not a finding about buyers, not a theory of how marketing works, but a way of sorting the decisions a firm controls. That is what the critics attacked, and it is why the framework cannot be falsified in the ordinary sense.

## What the evidence shows

There are two bodies of evidence. One is about adoption. The other is about effect.

**Adoption.** The framework spread through textbooks. By the 14th edition of Marketing Management (2012), Kotler and Keller were presenting McCarthy's four groups and proposing an updated set, people, processes, programs and performance, alongside them [22].

Booms and Bitner extended it to seven for services in 1981, adding people, process and physical evidence [4]. Kotler added two in 1986 for markets where a firm must win entry before it can compete: "executives must add two more", he wrote, "power and public relations" [5]. Rafiq and Ahmed's 1995 survey of UK and European marketing academics reported "a high degree of dissatisfaction with 4Ps" and "a high degree of acceptance" of the seven-P version [9].

The most useful adoption data is in The CMO Survey. In February 2018, 362 senior US marketers (98.3 per cent VP level or above) were asked which activities marketing leads in their company. Marketing led brand in 91.4 per cent of firms and advertising in 81.7 per cent; pricing in 25.8 per cent and distribution in 10.2 per cent [15, Table 9.1]. Of the four Ps, marketing departments own one.

**Effect.** The mix as a classification has never been tested empirically, because a classification makes no prediction. The elements have been measured, over and over.

The cleanest single study is Ataman, van Heerde and Mela (2010): a dynamic linear transfer function model on five years of advertising and scanner data for 70 brands in 25 categories in France, estimating the total (short-run plus long-run) sales elasticity of each element. Product 1.37, distribution 0.74, advertising 0.13, discounting 0.04 [11]. Discounting's long-run effects were one third of its short-run effects; for the other three, long-run effects were more than four times short-run [11].

The meta-analyses point the same way. Bijmolt, van Heerde and Pieters (2005): 1,851 price elasticities from 81 studies, mean minus 2.62 [12]. Sethuraman, Tellis and Briesch (2011): 751 short-term and 402 long-term advertising elasticities from 56 studies, means 0.12 and 0.24, declining over time [13]. Albers, Mantrala and Sridhar (2010): 506 personal-selling elasticities from 75 articles, mean 0.34 [14]. Different studies, different data, so the comparison is indicative. But the order is stable: price moves sales far more per percentage point than any form of promotion, and promotion is the element marketers most often control [15].

McKinsey's arithmetic on the income statement of a typical S&P 1500 company puts the same order in profit terms: a price rise of 1 per cent, volume held, lifts operating profit by 8 per cent, nearly 50 per cent more than a 1 per cent cut in variable costs and more than three times a 1 per cent rise in volume [28]. Price is the lever with the most leverage and the one marketing holds least often.

## The challenge

The critique has three strands, and only one of them is empirical.

**The framework is producer-centred.** Grönroos (1994), in Management Decision, argued that "the simplicity of the marketing mix paradigm, with its Four P model, has become a straitjacket, fostering toolbox thinking rather than an awareness that marketing is a multi-faceted social process" [8]. His evidence was the services and industrial marketing literature, where the buyer takes part in production and the relationship, not the transaction, is the unit of analysis. Lauterborn made the same point for a trade audience in 1990: "It's time to retire McCarthy's famous Four P's," replacing product, price, place and promotion with consumer wants and needs, cost to satisfy, convenience to buy, and communication [6]. Lauterborn's is a renaming, not a finding; he offered no data.

**The classification is badly built.** Van Waterschoot and Van den Bulte (1992), in the Journal of Marketing, tested McCarthy's four categories against Hunt's criteria for a classification and found them wanting: not mutually exclusive, not collectively exhaustive, and sales promotion defined negatively, as whatever is left over [7]. A logical test, not an empirical one, but the closest the literature comes to testing the framework itself. Constantinides (2006) reviewed the critique across six marketing fields and found two limitations common to all: "the model's internal orientation and lack of personalisation" [10].

**The mix says nothing about how buyers behave.** This is the Ehrenberg-Bass position, a different kind of objection. Sharp's [How Brands Grow](/readings/how-brands-grow-byron-sharp/) (2010) rests, in the institute's own description, on "scientific laws about buying and brand performance" that hold across categories regardless of what any firm does with its mix [16]. Place becomes physical availability, "the brand being easy to find and buy": presence, prominence and portfolio [17]. Promotion becomes the building of mental availability through distinctive assets [18]. An institute web page says its researchers "scrutinised the marketing mix, or the 4Ps model" and that such models "now lack the empirical support necessary to address the complexities of modern marketing" [26].

What is contested. Grönroos would replace the mix; van Waterschoot and Van den Bulte would repair it; Rafiq and Ahmed say the seven-P version already has. Ehrenberg-Bass does not argue about the boxes; it argues the boxes are the wrong place to start. None of this has been settled by data, because the disagreement is about what marketing is for.

## Where practitioners get it wrong

**Running the mix as a promotion plan.** The CMO Survey table is the misapplication in one place. If marketing leads advertising in four firms out of five and distribution in one in ten [15], the mix is not being managed as a mix. It is the fourth P with the other three set elsewhere. Every "marketing plan" that is a media plan with a product paragraph at the front is this error. The pattern has not moved. In every edition of the survey from March 2023 to 2026, marketing was primarily responsible for advertising in 83 to 92 per cent of companies, new products in 29 to 33 per cent, pricing in 25 to 31 per cent and distribution in 4 to 8 per cent [23, 24, 29, 30].

**Spending where the elasticity is lowest.** Ataman and colleagues found the two elements with the smallest long-run effects, advertising and discounting, were the two that had dominated the prior literature [11]. Binet and Field's IPA work makes the same point inside promotion: the optimum split they report between brand building and activation is 60:40, and the pull in most organisations is towards activation [19, 20]. Discounting has long-run effects one third the size of its short-run effects [11]. It looks like it works because the measurement window is short. Gartner's 2025 CMO Spend Survey shows where the money goes. Paid media is the largest line in the marketing budget at 30.6 per cent, digital channels take 61.1 per cent of total marketing spend, and the three largest digital lines are paid search, display and social advertising [25, 27]. Every one of them is the fourth P.

**Treating the four boxes as four equal boxes.** McCarthy's structure has no weights. Nothing in it says product matters more than price. The evidence does [11, 12, 13], and a plan that spends a page on each P is ignoring it. This is the "toolbox thinking" Grönroos warned about [8]: the boxes get filled because they are there.

Cialdini enters here, and only here. His seven principles, reciprocation, liking, social proof, authority, scarcity, commitment and consistency, and unity, are mechanisms of the fourth P [21, chapters 2 to 8]. They tell you how a promotion persuades, not whether promotion was the right lever. A marketer who has read Influence and not Ataman will pull the wrong one with great skill.

**Our own observation.** A residential developer with a fifteen-year portfolio briefed us for media: five projects, one new launch, a market that had just turned cautious. The problem was not the fourth P. For the established capital-city project demand existed, and the job was to capture it at a stable cost per enquiry. For the new coastal launch nobody was searching, because the thing had no name yet, so before any media ran we built a forty-eight-term keyword architecture in four intent groups. The launch scaled more than ninefold in a quarter while the established project held its cost per result. The developer brand, the one asset that should have carried all five projects, was the least communicated of the lot.

## What to do with it

1. Write down who in your company sets each of the four Ps. If marketing sets fewer than three, call your plan a communications plan, not a marketing mix. 2. Before any promotion budget is approved, list the distribution and product changes considered and rejected, with reasons. Ataman's elasticities [11] put the burden of proof on the advertiser. 3. Measure every price promotion over at least twelve months and report the long-run effect next to the short-run one. No long-run number, no evaluation. 4. Replace "place" in your plan with the three physical-availability questions: where does buying happen, are we easy to find there, and do we have a buyable product for that occasion [17]. 5. Split the promotion line into brand and activation and report the ratio quarterly. Below 60:40 in favour of brand with no stated reason is the finding [19, 20]. 6. Delete the word "mix" from any plan that does not show the four elements with a weight next to each. Unweighted, it is a list. 7. When a colleague proposes another P, ask which decision it would change. Booms and Bitner's three did, for service firms [4]. Most later additions did not.

### Positioning in marketing

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/principles/positioning-in-marketing/
Date: 2026-09-05. Read: 10 min.

Positioning, as Ries and Trout set it out in 1972, claims that a brand wins by occupying one clear slot in the prospect's memory [2][3]. The memory half holds up. The difference half does not. Across 17 categories in two countries, only 17% of a brand's own buyers called it different or unique, and they kept buying anyway [8]. Practitioners should stop testing whether buyers believe the difference, start measuring whether they can recognise the brand, and put the budget behind reach and consistency.

## Origin

Jack Trout published the first article to use the term in June 1969, in Industrial Marketing, under the title "'Positioning' is a game people play in today's me-too market place" [1]. Its argument: a company can spend millions on great advertising and still fail if it ignores what already sits in the buyer's head [1]. Three years later Trout and Al Ries wrote the three-part series "The [Positioning Era Cometh](/history-of-advertising/1972-the-positioning-era/)" for Advertising Age (24 April, 1 May and 8 May 1972) [2]; the book, Positioning: The Battle for Your Mind, followed from McGraw-Hill in 1981 [3].

The 1972 text names the problem: the creative party of the 1960s was over and "the wreckage is still washing up on the beach" (Corfam, Gablinger's beer, Look magazine) [2]. Their answer, in their own words: the new era "stresses the need to create a 'position' in the prospect's mind" [2].

They were not alone. The same series quotes an Ogilvy advertisement of the period: "The results of your campaign depend less on how we write your advertising than on how your product is positioned" [2]. Ries and Trout gave the idea a theory: the overcommunicated society, the ladder in the mind, positioning against the leader as Avis did [1][2].

Two things to hold onto. It is a theory of communication, not of product: the 1969 article says the competitor's image "is just as important as your own. Sometimes more important" [1]. And it came from agency casework, not from a dataset. The textbook version is broader. Kotler and Keller made positioning the third step of segmentation, targeting and positioning, with a chapter titled "Crafting the Brand Positioning" [4]. Aaker folded it into brand identity, as the part that is actively communicated [5]. Keller, Sternthal and Tybout added the frame of reference, points of parity and points of difference [6][7].

## What the evidence shows

Here is the awkward part. Positioning as Ries and Trout wrote it has never been tested as a proposition. It is a theorist's claim built on cases: Avis, and 7-Up's Un-Cola, which the 1972 series says lifted sales "something like 10%" in its first year [2]. There is no controlled study we can cite that shows brands with a sharper position grow faster.

What has been tested is the claim underneath it: that buyers hold a perceived, valued difference in mind and buy because of it. The best direct test is Romaniuk, Sharp and Ehrenberg (2007) [8]. Method: telephone surveys in seven Australian categories (skincare, spirits, cars, beer, fast food, banking, supermarkets), with "different" and "unique" hidden at random among other attributes, plus Young & Rubicam Brand Asset Valuator data from ten UK categories collected in 1999 [8]. Only current users of each brand were counted.

Headline finding: across all 17 markets, an average of 11% of a brand's own users said it was different, 10% said it was unique, and 17% said either [8, Table 2]. Spirits and skincare, chosen for being image-led and heavily advertised, scored highest at 36% and 30%.

Two checks matter. Respondents were not apathetic: 54% named at least one brand in the category as different or unique, and 76% did so in soft drinks, while only 19% of Coca-Cola's users said it of Coca-Cola [8]. And brands with an obvious functional difference did score. Aldi, which does not stock national brands, got 67% for different from its own shoppers; Subway got 50% for unique against burger, pizza and chicken rivals [8]. Buyers can see difference when it is large. They mostly do not see it.

Business buyers are no sharper. A Gartner survey of more than 1,100 B2B customers in December 2020 found that 64% could not tell one B2B brand's digital experience from another's, and 76% did nothing different after engaging suppliers through websites, tools and content [16].

Apple is the authors' test case. In 1999, with coloured iMacs against beige boxes and its own operating system, 23% of Apple users called it different or unique. 77% did not [8, Table 5].

A second, older finding sits underneath this one. Bird, Channon and Ehrenberg (1970) showed that the share of people who attach an image attribute to a brand depends on how recently they used it [10]. Romaniuk, Bogomolova and Dall'Olmo Riley re-tested it in 2012 across new categories, countries and online data, and found the generalisation "still holds, both qualitatively and, to a large extent, quantitatively" [11]. The 2007 differentiation data show the same shape: users were roughly twice as likely as non-users to call a brand different [8, Table 4].

This is why an image tracker will always tell a big brand it is well positioned. Usage produces image responses, almost regardless of the attribute.

The third body of evidence is about what advertising does when it works. Binet and Field's analyses of the IPA Databank (880 cases in 2007 [12], 996 cases in 2013 [13]) find that campaigns which build fame, meaning the brand gets talked about, convert share of voice into growth most efficiently. On IPA cases from 2004 to 2016, rational campaigns returned a share-of-voice efficiency of 0.2, emotional campaigns 1.0, fame campaigns 1.3 [14]. Their reading of positioning's job matches Ehrenberg-Bass's: get the brand into more heads, rather than argue the point of difference to a few.

## The challenge

The strongest published critique comes from the same 2007 paper. Romaniuk, Sharp and Ehrenberg conclude that "marketers do not need to convince buyers that the brand is different in order to get them to buy" and that "such a task is probably near impossible" [8]. They put distinctiveness in differentiation's place: unique brand associations (colour, logo, tagline, character, advertising style) whose only job is to make the brand easy to notice and identify. The criteria are uniqueness and prevalence: linked to one brand only, and known to most buyers [8]. Sharp's [How Brands Grow](/readings/how-brands-grow-byron-sharp/) (2010) put it more bluntly: "Rather than striving for meaningful, perceived differentiation, marketers should seek meaningless distinctiveness. Branding lasts, differentiation doesn't" [9].

Read carefully, the two camps disagree less than the slogans suggest.

Where they agree: the contest happens in memory, not in the product. Ries and Trout said so in 1972 [2]; Romaniuk and colleagues say distinctive elements "create, refresh or reinforce consumer memory structures" [8]. Both insist the position, or the asset, must belong to one brand only. Both prize consistency over decades; the 2007 paper's example is the Nike swoosh, shown beside the name for years before it could stand alone [8].

Where they disagree: whether the thing in memory has to be a valued difference. Ries and Trout's position is a reason to prefer: Avis over Hertz, Un-Cola over cola. Ehrenberg-Bass says the memory structure need carry no meaning at all. It is a handle for retrieval, and buyers who cannot name anything different about the brand buy it regardless [8].

Kantar's own data lands between the camps. Its Blueprint for Brand Growth, built on 6.5 billion data points across 21,000 brands, decomposes demand into three drivers: salience explains 42%, meaning 38%, difference 20%. The same deck puts perceived relative difference at 50% of what justifies a brand's price [17]. Difference does little to get a brand bought and a great deal to get it paid for.

Where it is contested: Keller's camp holds that points of difference still matter once points of parity are met, and warns that "points of differentiation alone are not enough to sustain a brand against competitors" [6]. The 2007 paper cites that warning with approval [8]. The open question is whether the exceptions (Aldi, Subway and the small premium brands that scored higher [8]) show that real functional difference pays, or only that buyers can report a difference when it is large. Romaniuk and colleagues write that their data "does not totally negate" a causal link between perceived differentiation and performance, only that any gain looks temporary or quickly matched [8].

Ask buyers directly and the parity list is long. In Edelman's 2025 survey of 15,042 people in 15 countries, 88% called best quality, good value and "I trust it" important or a deal breaker for the brands they buy, and the next five attributes sat within eight points of them [18].

Cialdini did not address positioning by name. The nearest mechanism in Influence is the contrast principle in chapter 1: a second item is judged against the first, which is why an estate agent shows a run-down "setup" house before the real one [15]. It explains why "We're only No. 2" works as a claim: it borrows the leader's size as the contrast. It says nothing about owning a word, and we will not stretch it.

## Where practitioners get it wrong

The positioning statement that never leaves the deck. It is written once, approved, and then handed to a campaign with a new look every year. The 2007 paper's complaint is exactly this: consistency of message gets discussed, consistency of "the visual, verbal or style of branding elements" does not, and "most of the attention from marketers is on aspects that are new and fresh" [8]. The buyer never sees the position. They see six unconnected campaigns.

Reading the perceptual map as proof. Mapping techniques "highlight small differences, almost regardless of magnitude" [8]. Because usage drives image responses [10][11], the map mostly shows who has more users. A big brand looks well positioned on every axis. A small brand looks lost. Neither reading tells you what to say.

Manufacturing a difference the category cannot see. If your direct measure of "different" sits near the category norm of about 17% [8], and there is no Aldi-sized functional fact behind the claim, spend will move that number very little. The money does more work on reach, fame and a recognisable asset [8][14].

**Our own observation.** For a national membership platform for specialist physicians practising outside insurance, the temptation was a fresh angle every week; the subject is rich enough for it. We locked the assets instead: one belief line, one rhetorical device, one shape of invitation, the founders' actual faces, the same visual codes everywhere. Adopters then grew around 50% a month for three consecutive months with no paid acquisition behind it. The rate flatters a small base and will come down. The point holds: repetition built the memory, and the position never moved.

## What to do with it

1. Write the position in three lines: the frame of reference, the points of parity you must match, and one point of difference [6]. If any line is blank, the document is not finished. 2. Test the difference before spending on it. Ask current buyers, in a pick-any survey with "different" and "unique" buried among other attributes, whether the brand is either. Compare the result with the 17% average across 17 markets [8]. At or below that norm, stop trying to move it. 3. Pick two or three distinctive assets (a colour, a shape, a phrase, a character) and measure each with buyers on uniqueness and prevalence [8]. If fewer than half of your buyers link the asset to you alone, it is not yet an asset. 4. Freeze those assets for five years. Judge every new campaign on one question: would someone who saw the last one know this is the same brand? 5. Split every image tracker by usage before reading it [10][11]. Never present an all-respondent image score as evidence of position. 6. Put the budget behind reach and fame, not persuasion of the difference. Fame campaigns converted share of voice to growth at 1.3 against 0.2 for rational ones [14]. Keep share of voice at or above share of market [13]. 7. Position against the leader only when the contrast is true and checkable. Avis was second and said so [1]. If your claim depends on the buyer not knowing who leads, it is comparative advertising, not a position.

### Market segmentation

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/principles/market-segmentation/
Date: 2026-09-01. Read: 9 min.

Market segmentation claims a market is not one demand curve but several, and that a firm does better serving some of them well than all of them adequately [1]. The evidence supports that claim for categories: buyers differ in what they want and how much they use. It does not support it for brands. Across decades of panel data, competing brands are bought by the same kinds of people [8][10][11], and campaigns that address the whole market outperform tightly targeted ones [13]. Segment the category to shape the offer. Market the brand to everyone who buys the category.

## Origin

Wendell R. Smith set the idea out in July 1956, in the Journal of Marketing, volume 21, number 1, pages 3 to 8 [1]. The title says what he was doing: "Product Differentiation and Market Segmentation as Alternative Marketing Strategies". American firms in the mid 1950s faced imperfect competition and a market that no longer behaved like one homogeneous mass. Smith's contribution was to name two ways of responding, and to argue they were different strategies rather than the same thing under two labels. The distinction was still muddled thirty years later: Dickson and Ginter opened their 1987 paper by noting "considerable misunderstanding about their meaning and use" [5].

His definition, on page 6: segmentation means "viewing a heterogeneous market as a number of smaller homogeneous markets" [1][2].

The idea entered the mainstream in two steps. Daniel Yankelovich's 1964 Harvard Business Review article argued that demographics had lost predictive power and that segmentation should also consider "buyer attitudes, motivations, values, patterns of usage, aesthetic preferences, and degree of susceptibility", across ten consumer and industrial markets [3]. Yoram Wind's 1978 review in the Journal of Marketing Research codified the method: problem definition, research design, data collection, analysis, interpretation and implementation [4]. That is a review of how to segment, not a test of whether segments predict brand choice.

The paper is six pages long and is still cited every year, seventy years on.

Philip Kotler's Marketing Management, first published in 1967 [6], turned the idea into the sequence every marketing graduate learns: segment, target, position. Kotler and Keller's current editions list four bases for consumer segmentation, geographic, demographic, psychographic and behavioural. David Aaker's Strategic Market Management places segmentation inside customer analysis, the first question a strategist asks about a market [7]. Robert Cialdini did not address segmentation. Influence describes principles of compliance that operate across people and offers no view on whether different segments need different principles [15].

## What the evidence shows

The record is uneven. Segmentation is one of the most used tools in marketing and one of the least tested at the level that matters to a brand owner. The literature from Yankelovich to Wind is methodological [3][4]. It tells you how to find segments. It rarely asks whether the segments a brand targets contain different people from the ones it does not.

Two things are well supported.

First, categories are heterogeneous. Buyers differ in usage rate, occasion and need, and Smith's point about "divergent demand" [2] stands. Nobody in the debate below disputes it.

Second, breadth of targeting predicts business results. Les Binet and Peter Field analysed the IPA Effectiveness Databank, which at the time held 996 campaigns entered for the IPA Effectiveness Awards from 1980 to 2010, covering more than 700 brands in over 80 categories [13]. Campaigns that targeted the whole market reported on average 1.8 very large business effects and 6.7 very large effects in total. Campaigns aimed at new customers reported 1.7 and 5.4. Campaigns aimed at existing customers reported 0.6 and 2.4 [13, Figure 18].

Efficiency moves the same way, only more sharply. Measured as annualised market share growth per ten points of excess share of voice, whole-market campaigns scored 2.6, new-customer campaigns 0.3 and existing-customer campaigns 0.2 [13, Figure 21]. Binet and Field's own summary: "the benefits of broad reach considerably outweigh the benefits of tight targeting: a finding that directly contradicts much of the current orthodoxy" [13].

The loyalty finding is the sharpest. Only 12 percent of IPA campaigns that set out to increase loyalty achieved a very large loyalty effect, against 47 percent of acquisition campaigns that achieved very large penetration growth [13]. Their 2017 update, Media in Focus, re-ran the analysis on 2008 to 2016 cases and found the same ordering for annual market share growth: campaigns addressing both new and existing customers grew share fastest, new-customer campaigns next, existing-customer campaigns least [14, Figure 14]. By 2014 to 2016, pure loyalty campaigns had fallen to 3 percent of IPA entries [14].

One caveat is ours, not theirs. The Databank is built from award entries. Whole-market campaigns may also be the ones with the biggest brands behind them. The share-of-voice measure controls for spend, but the cases are not a random sample of marketing activity.

## The challenge

The strongest published critique comes from the Ehrenberg-Bass Institute, and it is narrower than it is usually reported. It does not say segments do not exist. It says brands do not own them.

Hammond, Ehrenberg and Goodhardt put it to the test in 1996 in the European Journal of Marketing. Using consumer panel data across more than 20 grocery categories in several countries, they found "little brand segmentation": the profiles of competing brands' buyers differed little on the usual socio-demographic measures, and brands in the same category "tend to be bought by similar kinds of people" [8]. They also noted that "few, if any, examples of marked brand segmentation are cited in the literature" [8]. Kennedy and Ehrenberg gave the finding its blunt title in 2001, "There is no brand segmentation", in Marketing Research [9].

The finding has been re-tested rather than left alone. Uncles, Kennedy, Nenycz-Thiel, Singh and Kwok re-examined it in 2012 with newer data, extending the scope to brands in emerging markets, private labels, variants and composite segments, and reported that "despite attempts by marketers to differentiate brands and provide customized features for distinct target audiences", user profiles of directly competing brands seldom differ [10]. Anesbury, Winchester and Kennedy added the time dimension in 2017: profiles seldom differ between brands and seldom change over years [11].

Byron Sharp gave the finding a chapter title in [How Brands Grow](/readings/how-brands-grow-byron-sharp/), "Our buyers are different", and a second chapter on competition, "Who do you really compete with?" [12]. His examples run from Ford and Chevrolet owners in the 1950s to UK car owners in the 1990s, whose agreement with attitude statements barely moved across brands [12]. The institute's later B2B work, on infrastructure-as-a-service, business intelligence and CRM software, claims the same law holds there: "the only meaningful difference in the customer base is its size, not its composition" [16]. The institute's business intelligence data, published with the LinkedIn B2B Institute, show what that means in practice: 80 percent of Amplitude's customers also use Google, and on average 68 percent of any brand's customers also buy AWS, so the buyers a small brand calls its own are mostly the big brands' buyers too [19].

What is contested, and by whom. Segmentation's defenders hold that the Ehrenberg-Bass tests use the wrong variables: demographics and broad attitudes were never the bases a good segmentation would use, and needs- or occasion-based segments would show differences these tests cannot see. Uncles and colleagues acknowledge "potential boundary conditions" in their abstract [10]. The Ehrenberg-Bass reply is that whatever the basis, the brands end up with the same buyers, so the segment describes the category, not the brand. The literature has not resolved this. The two sides measure different things: who the brand wanted, and who the brand got.

## Where practitioners get it wrong

Three misapplications recur.

Personas become media plans. A segmentation built to sharpen the offer is handed to the media team, who buy only the audience the persona describes. The persona was a design tool. Used as an exclusion rule, it cuts reach, the variable Binet and Field found matters most [13]. The narrowing also fails on its own terms: in Nielsen's benchmark of more than 44,000 digital campaigns, about half of the impressions aimed at a broad age and gender group reached it, and only about a fifth of those aimed at one gender in a narrow age range did [17].

"Our buyer is different." Brand teams compare their buyer to a stereotype of the competitor's buyer rather than to the category's buyer. When the comparison is run on the same variables, on panel data, the difference is usually within a few percentage points [8][10]. The belief survives because nobody runs the comparison.

Loyalty first. Budgets tilt toward existing customers because they are cheaper to reach and easier to measure. The Databank says these campaigns produce the smallest effects and the lowest efficiency of any targeting choice [13][14].

**Our own observation.** A European supply chain services group asked us to open two markets where the category itself was unfamiliar. We ran one message identically in both, so the variable was the market and not the copy. Two countries, different languages, different competitors, different maturity, and category search presence landed within a point of each other inside sixty days. The consistency was the finding, not the level. Had those buyers needed two segment-specific arguments, the numbers would have said so. They did not.

Buyers do ask to be understood: in Salesforce's 2022 survey of 13,020 consumers and 3,916 business buyers, 73 percent expected companies to understand their unique needs, up from 66 percent in 2020, while 56 percent said most companies still treat them as a number, which is a case for segmenting the offer and the service rather than the audience [18].

## What to do with it

1. Segment the category on behaviour first: usage frequency, occasion and need, from purchase or usage data. Record each segment's size as a share of category buyers. A segmentation document with no sizes is a persona deck. 2. Run the user-profile test once a year. Put your brand's buyer profile next to the category's on the same five to ten variables. If no variable differs by more than a few percentage points, remove the phrase "our target customer" from the brief and replace it with "category buyers". 3. Write the reach target as a share of all category buyers, with a number, in every brand-building brief. A brief with no reach figure is a brief that will be narrowed by default. 4. Split the budget by task. Brand building goes to the whole category through broad-reach media. Activation goes tightly targeted to people in market now, the line Binet and Field draw in Figure 01 of Media in Focus [14]. Keep the two on separate lines in the plan so one cannot absorb the other. 5. Use segments to change the offer: variants, price points, pack sizes, distribution. Do not use them to decide who is not allowed to see the advertising. 6. Re-check profiles every two to three years and expect them to be stable [11]. A profile that moves a lot is a measurement problem before it is a strategy result. 7. Report penetration before loyalty in every quarterly review, and report both against the category, not against last quarter.

### Unique selling proposition (USP)

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/principles/unique-selling-proposition/
Date: 2026-08-27. Read: 11 min.

Rosser Reeves set out the unique selling proposition in 1961 as a three-part rule: every advertisement must offer a specific benefit, competitors must not claim it, and it must be strong enough to pull new buyers [1]. His evidence was agency data. Published work since points the other way: buyers of most brands do not see them as different [4], rational-claim campaigns report very large profit effects less often than emotional ones [5], and the industry's own effectiveness data put the work on creative quality and trust rather than on the claim [8, 11, 12]. Keep the discipline of one clear claim. Drop the belief that uniqueness sells.

## Origin

Reeves, chairman of Ted Bates & Company, published Reality in Advertising with Alfred A. Knopf in 1961. He wrote that the theory "originated at Ted Bates & Company in the early 1940's" [1, ch. 13]. The problem was waste. Bates had been splitting the population into people who remembered a campaign and people who did not, then measuring how many in each group used the product [1, ch. 3]. Penetration: the share of the population who remember your current advertising. Usage pull: the difference in product usage between those who remember it and those who do not [1, ch. 3].

The definition comes in chapter 13, "The Copy Leverage", where he complains that U.S.P. had become "perhaps the most misused series of letters in advertising" and gives it three parts [1, ch. 13]. First: "Each advertisement must make a proposition to the consumer." Second, the proposition must be one "that the competition either cannot, or does not, offer". Third, it "must be so strong that it can move the mass millions, i.e., pull over new customers to your product" [1, ch. 13]. He shows condition two failing alone with a toothpaste that advertised "it comes out like a ribbon and lies flat on your brush": unique, and useless [1, ch. 13].

The USP is not a slogan, and Reeves says so. It is a product claim chosen because the Bates data said such claims produced the most usage pull. So that data is the first question.

## What the evidence shows

Reeves' own evidence. The Bates studies covered "seventy-eight of the biggest package-goods advertisers in the United States", with budgets from $400,000 to $17,500,000 a year [1, chs. 3 and 4]. Penetration ran from 1% to 78% of the population [1, ch. 4]. His summary statistic: companies applying his principles achieved penetration 15.4% above the competing-brand average and usage pull 16.2% above, which he multiplies into a 34% advantage [1, ch. 6].

Treat these numbers as what they are: agency data on the agency's own clients, never published in a journal, with no sampling detail, no confidence intervals, anonymous brands and no replication. One more problem, our reading rather than a published one. People who already use a product are more likely to remember its advertising, so part of the gap between rememberers and non-rememberers is caused by usage rather than causing it. Reeves reports a correlation and calls it pull.

The peer-reviewed record supports something narrower. Ehrenberg's 1974 paper in the Journal of Advertising Research reviewed the buying-behaviour evidence for frequently bought goods and found no evidence that advertising "actually works by any strong form of persuasion" [2]. His sequence is awareness, trial, reinforcement: "for frequently bought products, repeat buying is the main determinant of sales volume and here advertising must be reinforcing rather than persuasive" [2]. That answers Reeves' third condition directly. Reeves needs a claim strong enough to move new buyers. Ehrenberg's data say most volume comes from existing buyers being reminded.

The one part of Reeves that later evidence supports is staying with a campaign. He called too-frequent change "the multi-million dollar error" and reported a dental cream campaign running twenty-two years while holding first place [1, ch. 8]. Ehrenberg's model predicts that outcome, for a different reason.

The language has moved on without him. Romaniuk, Sharp and Ehrenberg summarise Kotler's Marketing Management as talking "of a meaningful perceived difference that provides buyers with their reason to purchase" [4, p. 43]. Kotler places the USP inside positioning, as one answer to how many benefits to promote, under a wider value proposition. Aaker's Building Strong Brands (1996) treats the functional benefit as one layer of a brand identity that also carries emotional and self-expressive benefits, and warns against fixing on product attributes [6]. Ries and Trout, in their 1972 Advertising Age series and 1981 book, moved the battleground from the product to the prospect's mind [7]. Their debt to Reeves is the single message; their departure is that it is built from perception, not a product claim.

## The challenge

Two published bodies of evidence cut against the USP, at different conditions.

Romaniuk, Sharp and Ehrenberg (2007) went after the second condition, uniqueness. They asked current users whether the brand they buy is "different" or "unique", across seven Australian categories collected by telephone and ten UK categories from Young & Rubicam's 1999 Brand Asset Valuator survey, 17 markets in all [4, pp. 45-46]. Averaged across those markets, 11% of a brand's own users said it was different, 10% said unique and 17% said either [4, Table 2]. Brands with an obvious functional difference scored higher: Aldi, 67% for different [4, p. 46]. Apple, "often presented as a poster child for differentiation", still had 77% of its users not perceiving it as different or unique [4, p. 48]. The authors' conclusion: "less trying to find unique selling propositions and more trying to find unique identifying characteristics" [4, p. 52].

It measures stated perception, not what drives choice, mostly for established brands [4, p. 49]. What it removes is Reeves' second-condition assumption: that buyers of a successful brand carry a perceived unique reason to buy it. Mostly they do not.

Kantar reads the same question from the other side. Its BrandZ work with the Saïd Business School at Oxford modelled 872 brands from 2006 to 2022 and found perceived difference to be the leading brand factor in share-price outperformance, 35% of the brand effect against 0.6% for salience, and that Meaningful and Different together explain 94% of pricing power, salience 6% [10]. Read with Romaniuk: few buyers perceive a difference, but where they do, it is what lets the brand charge more. Neither result says a unique product claim is how that difference gets built. Kantar's own factor analysis puts 30% of difference on distinctive assets and the rest on positioning, product experience, service and advertising associations [10].

Binet and Field went after the mechanism. Their 2013 IPA report The Long and the Short of It analysed 996 campaigns from 700 brands across 83 categories in the IPA Databank [5]. Campaigns coded as rational (a product or price message) reported very large effects on sales in 46% of cases, against 55% for emotional campaigns; on market share 28% against 31%; on loyalty 5% against 11%; on price sensitivity 2% against 5%; on new customers the two tied at 27% [5, Figures 44, 53, 54]. Very large profit growth was reported by 16% of rational campaigns, 25% of combined and 29% of emotional [5]. The gap grows with time: at one year 13% of emotional campaigns against 10% of rational; at two years 30% against 20%; at three years or more 43% against 23% [5].

Two cautions. The IPA Databank is a set of award entries, so it over-represents campaigns that worked. And the rational versus emotional split is a coding of each campaign's dominant approach, not a controlled test. Binet and Field's own reading: rational messaging gives a big direct effect that decays quickly, emotional priming a smaller one that builds [5, slides 13 and 14].

The industry's own attribution work puts the weight in the same place. Nielsen Catalina Solutions decomposed the sales lift of nearly 500 FMCG campaigns run in 2016 and the first quarter of 2017 and attributed 47% of it to the creative, 22% to reach, 15% to brand factors such as price and penetration, 9% to targeting, 5% to recency and 2% to context [8]. Cannes Lions and WARC found the same from the other end: across 3,786 effectiveness award cases from 2011 to 2019, campaigns that had also won creative awards averaged 4.5 WARC effectiveness points against 2.6 for those that had not [13]. What both measure is the quality of the execution, not the presence of a claim.

Where the literature is split. Reeves and Ehrenberg agree that campaigns should not change often and that memory matters. They disagree on what memory does. Reeves: the remembered claim pulls new users. Ehrenberg: the remembered brand reassures existing ones. The Bates data cannot separate the two; it never distinguished new buyers from existing buyers who remembered the ad. Sharp and Romaniuk side with Ehrenberg, in chapter 8 of [How Brands Grow](/readings/how-brands-grow-byron-sharp/) [9]. Binet and Field sit between: rational claims work, for a while. Kantar's BrandZ data side with Reeves on whether difference pays and against him on how it is built [10]. No one has replicated Reeves' 34%.

Cialdini did not address the USP. His work matters because it names what a single rational claim leaves out. Social proof (chapter 4), authority (chapter 5) and scarcity (chapter 6) in the 2021 edition of Influence move buyers without any claim that the product is unique [3]. A queue, a credential and "only three left" are propositions of a different kind, each with an experimental literature behind it.

Edelman's 2019 brand-trust survey of 16,000 people in eight countries puts a number on what the claim leaves out. 81% said being able to trust the brand to do what is right was a deal breaker or a deciding factor in a purchase, in the same band as quality at 85%, convenience and value at 84% and ingredients at 82% [12]. The same survey found 13% had strong trust in a brand message after seeing it once and 87% after seeing it across six channels [12]. A proposition, however unique, is one message seen once.

## Where practitioners get it wrong

The slogan mistake. Reeves complained in 1961 that U.S.P. was being applied "to slogans, slick phrases, strange pictures, mere headlines" [1, ch. 13]. Sixty-five years later the output of a USP workshop is still a tagline, and a tagline the product cannot prove or disprove is not a proposition.

The uniqueness hunt. Teams spend months on a feature no competitor has, then find buyers do not value it (Reeves' toothpaste ribbon [1, ch. 13]) or cannot perceive it (the 17% in Romaniuk, Sharp and Ehrenberg [4]). The search eats the money that distinctive assets, consistent creative and reach would have used.

The forever-rational plan. Firms that take the USP literally build every campaign as a product claim and judge it on short-term response, where rational campaigns look best (very large direct effects: rational above combined above emotional [5, slide 32]) and where the three-year profit gap is invisible. The B2B Institute at LinkedIn and System1 rated 1,700 B2B ads on System1's five-star emotional-response scale: 76.7% scored one star, the level System1 associates with no market-share growth, and 0.5% scored four or five [11].

**Our own observation.** In the fourth month of a residential developer engagement we stopped buying attention and went to earn it: a full editorial interview with the chief executive in a sector trade publication, secured in the annual editorial plan without paying for placement, on the seven things the market was anxious about, pricing, cost pressure, regulation, and whether developers deliver what they promise. No unique product claim anywhere in it. In a market asking whether a developer will still exist at handover, third-party endorsement did work that no proposition about the product could.

## What to do with it

1. Write the claim in Reeves' form first: "Buy this, and you will get this specific benefit." If no testable benefit finishes the sentence, there is no proposition, only a slogan [1, ch. 13]. 2. Test the benefit for importance, not uniqueness. Ask current buyers, unprompted, why they buy. If fewer than one in five name the benefit, uniqueness will not rescue it [4]. 3. Expect low differentiation scores. Fewer than 20% of users calling a brand "different" is the norm across 17 markets [4, Table 2]. Put the budget into distinctive assets: name, colour, shape, sound, character, used identically everywhere [4, p. 52]. 4. Keep the rational claim in activation and hold it to activation metrics. Judge brand advertising on three-year profit, where emotional campaigns lead 43% to 23% [5], and test the execution before the claim: creative carried 47% of sales lift in Nielsen's decomposition [8]. 5. Change the claim rarely and the execution often. Reeves' one finding that has held is the cost of switching campaigns [1, ch. 8]; Ehrenberg explains why [2]. 6. When the product has no unique benefit, use Cialdini's levers instead of inventing one: visible customer numbers, credentials, real limits on supply [3, chs. 4 to 6]. Never fake the scarcity. 7. If anyone quotes Reeves' 34%, ask for the sampling method; the book has none [1, ch. 6].

### Mental availability and physical availability

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/principles/mental-and-physical-availability/
Date: 2026-08-22. Read: 10 min.

Sharp's claim is that brands grow by being easy to think of and easy to buy, because loyalty follows market share rather than causing it [1]. The second half is well tested: double jeopardy holds in 32 differentiated replications, in cars, business banking, aircraft and packaged goods [6][9][10]. The first half, that mental availability itself moves share, rests mostly on one institute. Practitioners should track penetration before any loyalty metric, stop expecting retention schemes to beat a law, and build memory links to buying situations rather than an awareness score.

## Origin

Byron Sharp published [How Brands Grow](/readings/how-brands-grow-byron-sharp/): What Marketers Don't Know with Oxford University Press in 2010 [1]. Chapter 12 carries the two terms. Mental availability is the probability that buyers "notice, recognize and/or think of a brand in buying situations" [1][2]. Physical availability is the ease of finding and buying it. The book's argument is that these two are what budgets should build. What "easy to buy" means has moved since 2010: in McKinsey's 2024 B2B Pulse survey of nearly 4,000 decision makers in 13 countries, buyers used an average of ten channels to interact with suppliers, up from five in 2016, and among sellers that offer e-commerce it now brings in 34% of revenue against 17% from in-person sales [30].

The problem Sharp was solving was a decade of loyalty-first management. Reichheld and Sasser had told Harvard Business Review readers in 1990 that "companies can boost profits by almost 100% by retaining just 5% more of their customers" [18], and Aaker's Managing [Brand Equity](/principles/brand-equity/) (1991) had put brand loyalty first among five equity assets [20]. Sharp's answer: brands do not grow by deepening loyalty, they grow by adding buyers.

The regularity underneath the book is double jeopardy, which William McPhee described in Formal Theories of Mass Behavior (1963) for actors, comic strips and radio presenters before anyone applied it to brands [5][9]. Ehrenberg, Goodhardt and Barwise formalised it for buying in the Journal of Marketing in 1990: "a small brand typically has far fewer buyers than a larger brand. In addition, its buyers tend to buy it less often" [6]. Uncles, Ehrenberg and Hammond (1995) tied the regularities together in the NBD-Dirichlet model [7]. Sharp's own step before the book was brand salience, defined with Jenni Romaniuk in 2004 as "the brand's propensity to be noticed or come to mind in buying situations" [8]. Mental availability is that idea renamed and widened. [How Brands Grow](/readings/how-brands-grow-byron-sharp/) Part 2 (2016) took the laws to emerging markets, services and luxury [3]; Romaniuk's Building Distinctive Brand Assets (2018) is the operating manual for the mental half [4].

## What the evidence shows

Ehrenberg, Goodhardt and Barwise (1990) reviewed the panel evidence, the theory and the known exceptions [6]. Graham, Bennett, Franke, Henfrey and Nagy-Hamada (2017) took the law into long-run continuous buying, emerging markets, capital purchasing and house-of-brands portfolios. Across 32 differentiated replications, some 35 years apart, they "find no boundary condition to the operation of the Double Jeopardy characteristic" [10].

The B2B evidence is the part a Brave New reader will want. Romaniuk, Dawes and Faghidno (2021) published an Ehrenberg-Bass report with new survey data on UK business banking and US business insurance, plus a table of eight earlier B2B studies [9]. In banking, Barclays, used by 41% of firms surveyed, held 5.7 of 17 possible products per customer and 27% solely loyal customers; Metro, used by 11%, held 3.2 products and 3% [9]. The report does not state its sample size.

The companion report in the same series asked 609 UK business banking buyers and 616 US business insurance buyers a second question, whether they would refuse to use each brand, and found the barrier to acquisition lies elsewhere: rejection averaged 11% across 22 UK banks and 7% across 17 US insurers, while the share of buyers unaware of a bank ran from 16% for Barclays to 80% for Handelsbanken [28]. A small B2B brand is small because most potential buyers do not know it, not because they have decided against it.

The durable B2B case is aircraft. Bennett, Anesbury and Graham (2018) used 9,000 purchase records from 51 airlines over ten years: Boeing, bought by 86% of airlines, averaged 101 purchases per buyer; Embraer, bought by 16%, averaged 37 [9][31].

Kim, Singh and Winer (2017) used A.C. Nielsen's US household panel, 2004 to 2009, and measured the share of each brand's dollar sales delivered by its top 20% of buyers across 238 brands in 22 categories, roughly 18,000 households [12]. The mean Pareto ratio was 0.73 with a standard deviation of 0.07; category averages ran from 0.64 for liquid detergent to 0.89 for cigarettes, and under Nielsen's narrower brand definition the mean fell to 0.65 [12]. They note the rule "is not precisely .80" [12].

Sharp and Graham read similar data differently. On Kantar data for about 600 UK brands in 40 categories, the top 20% deliver around 40% of sales in a quarter, "over 50%" in a year and "just over 60%" over five years, and 80% of a brand's buyers make five purchases or fewer in five years [13]. Both figures sit well below 80; the gap is windows and brand definitions.

The evidence for mental availability as a cause, rather than for double jeopardy as a pattern, is thinner. Romaniuk and Sharp (2004) set out the construct and a multi-cue measure [8]. Keller's customer-based [brand equity](/principles/brand-equity/) model (2001) had already put brand salience at the base of its pyramid: salience "influences the likelihood that the brand will be a member of the consideration set", with depth (ease of recall) and breadth (the range of situations in which the brand comes to mind) [21]. Breadth is mental availability under another name. Keller then builds meaning, feelings and resonance on top; Sharp treats salience plus distribution as the whole job.

Binet and Field's meta-analysis of 996 IPA Databank campaigns (2013) lands on Sharp's side for reach and elsewhere for mechanism. Their fame campaigns turned excess share of voice into growth at an annualised efficiency of 1.4 against 0.3 for other campaigns [23]. Reach is common ground. The mechanism is not: Sharp's account is memory refreshed, Binet and Field's is emotional priming that builds over years [23].

## The challenge

Three serious critiques and one loud one.

The first is the loyalty camp. Reichheld's numbers are claims from company casework, not panel findings; The Loyalty Effect (1996) says "even a small improvement in customer retention can double profits" [18][19]. Aaker's pyramid is a theorist's structure [20]. Neither has met double jeopardy on the same data and won.

The second is the academic critique of the Dirichlet's generality, and it comes from inside the model. Fader and Schmittlein (1993) showed across product markets in Japan and the United States that high-share brands have significantly more loyalty than the Dirichlet predicts, and traced it to consumer segments created partly by distribution [14]. Jung, Gruca and Rego (2010) replicated this across US packaged goods and found excess loyalty positively related to market share in 86% of categories, a pattern some authors call triple jeopardy [15]. Scriven, Bound and Graham (2017) sorted the recurring deviations in 62 FMCG categories into three types and concluded that "brand performance remains close to Dirichlet prediction" [16]. The model bends, it does not break, and when it bends it favours the big brand.

The third is scope. Sharp, Wright and Goodhardt (2002) themselves split repeat-purchase markets into repertoire markets, where the familiar patterns hold, and subscription markets such as insurance and banking, where most buyers use one brand at a time. The distinction "turns out to be an important boundary condition for some well-established generalisations", and their analysis "does not extend to markets for durable products" [11]. The B2B evidence since then is real but narrower than the FMCG base: two Ehrenberg-Bass surveys with unstated samples, one aircraft dataset, and eight older studies, six from before 2001 [9]. Double jeopardy travels. The full Dirichlet toolkit, and the claim that availability is the only lever worth funding, have been tested far less outside the supermarket. Formisano, Pauwels and Zarantonello (2020) put it this way: marketers should "not oversimplify Dirichlet evidences by thinking of availability as the only (costly) response to all marketing challenges" [17].

The loud one is Mark Ritson's 2018 Marketing Week column: Sharp's claim that it is "impossible" to value brand perceptions "is not just mistaken, it is a rejection of true scientific method" [27]. It added no data.

We could not confirm whether the 16th edition of Kotler, Keller and Chernev's Marketing Management (2021) covers double jeopardy or the Dirichlet at all [22]. Cialdini did not address mental availability. The availability heuristic the term echoes is Tversky and Kahneman's (1973), a rule about judging frequency from ease of recall [25]. The nearest Cialdini gets is Pre-Suasion (2016), chapters 2 and 3, on attention and the principle that "what's focal is causal"; that is attention in the moment of persuasion, not a brand's standing in memory across buying situations [24].

## Where practitioners get it wrong

Awareness is reported as mental availability. Sharp's 2011 note is blunt: recall and recognition scores are "flawed by the use of a single, a-situational, cue", usually the category name [2]. A brand can post high prompted awareness and still be absent from memory when a buyer needs a supplier for a specific job. The measure Romaniuk and Sharp propose uses one cue per buying situation [8].

Small brands are given loyalty KPIs. Double jeopardy says a 10% penetration brand will show lower loyalty than a 40% brand for no reason other than size [6][9]. A retention target set at the leader's number is one the law forbids. The loyalty-programme test in this literature is Sharp and Sharp (1997), which benchmarked a programme's repeat-purchase patterns against Dirichlet norms [26].

The 80/20 slide. Kim, Singh and Winer's mean is 0.73 over six years; Sharp and Graham's is around 0.40 in a quarter [12][13]. A plan that concentrates budget on the top fifth rests on a number the panel data does not produce.

**Our own observation.** In one of the supply chain group's established markets the brand had gone years without consistent presence and had slipped out of the consideration set, with the operation intact and the alternatives long-standing. Nothing about the service had changed. Its availability in buyers' memory had. Rebuilding it was a matter of presence, a weekly publishing rhythm per market, and the clearest lesson of the year was that consistency of spend mattered more than size of spend. Fragmented allocation stopped campaigns before they could compound. The industry survey closest to that experience is Edelman and LinkedIn's 2024 study of 3,484 executives in seven countries: 75% said a piece of thought leadership had sent them to research a product or service they had not been considering, and 86% of decision-makers said they would invite a company that consistently publishes good thought leadership into an RFP [29]. Presence gets a brand into the room; nothing else in the survey does.

## What to do with it

1. Put penetration, the share of category buyers who bought you in the period, on the first line of every brand dashboard, with loyalty metrics beneath it [6][9]. 2. Before setting a retention or share-of-wallet target, tabulate the category by penetration as Romaniuk, Dawes and Faghidno describe, and set the target where the double jeopardy line predicts for your size [9]. 3. Replace the single-cue awareness question with a battery of buying situations, ask which brands come to mind for each, and report the share of situations in which you are named [8]. 4. Classify your category as repertoire or subscription before choosing metrics; use purchase frequency and share of requirements in the first, defection and tenure in the second [11]. 5. Test the Pareto ratio on your own customer file at one quarter, one year and three years, and stop using any figure you did not compute [12][13]. 6. List every place and moment a buyer could look for you, mark each yes or no, and fix the noes before spending on anything else in this article.

### The Long and the Short of It

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/principles/the-long-and-the-short-of-it/
Date: 2026-08-18. Read: 10 min.

Binet and Field claim that advertising works in two modes on two clocks: activation sells now and fades, brand building sells later and compounds, so budgets should lean long, at roughly 60:40 [1]. The evidence is 996 award entries in which volume arrives within months, pricing power takes years, and efficiency peaks at 30 to 50 percent activation [1]. The ratio ranges from 46:54 to 74:26 by context, and nobody has replicated it on independent data [5][6]. Keep the two-clock model. Drop the number as a target. Measure the long effect directly.

## Origin

Les Binet and Peter Field published *The Long and the Short of It* through the IPA in 2013, funded by Thinkbox, the UK commercial television body [1, p7]. Their 2007 report *Marketing in the Era of Accountability* had noticed that campaigns scoring best on profit and share scored worst on short-term response, but lacked the data to pursue it [1, p18][2]. By 2013 the IPA Effectiveness Databank held 996 campaigns entered into the awards between 1980 and 2010, covering more than 700 brands in over 80 categories, and since 2008 entrants had been asked how long their campaign ran [1, p10-11].

The problem was quarterly reporting and instant online metrics pushing marketers to judge everything on a short window that, the authors argued, hid most of the value [1, p7, p9]. The headline claim is stated with care: "the optimum balance of brand and activation expenditure is on average around 60:40" [1, p9]. The same sentence adds that this "may vary by category".

## What the evidence shows

Every number comes from IPA award entries (a confidential questionnaire since 1998, coded from the written cases before that), scored on a three-point scale, with only top-box ("very large") effects counted [1, p10-12]. Of the 996 cases, 760 had a coded duration, 690 reported business effects and 171 had the data for the efficiency metric [1, Table 2, p11].

**Volume is fast, pricing is slow.** The share of cases reporting very large sales growth is 23 percent at three months and 36 percent at three years or more. The share reporting very large pricing effects is zero at three months and 3.1 percent at three years. Profit sits between: 4 percent at three months, 15 percent at three years [1, Figs 11-13, p19].

**The 60:40 finding.** The authors sorted UK media into brand channels and activation channels and found UK spend divided 61:39 between them in 2011 [1, Fig 34, p37]. They then grouped cases by activation share of budget. Annualised efficiency (share growth per year per 10 points of extra share of voice) was 0.5 below 30 percent activation, 1.3 in the 30 to 50 percent band, and 0.5 above 50 percent [1, Fig 37, p39]. The count of very large effects peaked near 40 percent activation [1, Fig 38, p39]. Footnote 13 reads: "The volume of data for this analysis is limited, so the finding is somewhat tentative and it is not possible to explore how this varies by category" [1, p39].

**Emotional work compounds.** Among rational campaigns, 10 percent reported very large profit growth at one year, 20 at two, 23 at three or more. Among emotional campaigns: 13, 30 and 43 percent [1, Fig 52, p53]. The curves cross at roughly six months; judged on a shorter window, rational work looks more profitable [1, p53].

**The follow-ups narrowed the claim.** *Media in Focus* (2017) reran the media analysis on 497 for-profit cases from 1998 onwards, restated 60:40 as "typically optimal", and documented the drift: cases evaluated over less than six months rose from a long-run 8 percent to about 25 percent, and cases with activation objectives went from 47 percent before the financial crisis to 72 percent in the four years to 2016 [4, Fig 51]. *Effectiveness in Context* put the all-case optimum at 62:38, footnoted as "unlikely to be statistically significant from 60:40", then broke it by context [5, p7]. The optimum brand share runs from 55 percent (low online-research categories, offline brands) to 74 (high-research categories, online and subscription brands) [5, Figs 16, 19, 26, 32]. The B2B analysis, on fewer than 50 cases, found 46:54 [6].

Outside the databank, two findings support the two-clock model without supporting any ratio. Lodish and colleagues tracked 55 in-market TV weight tests for two years after the test year: where year one showed a significant effect, the next two years added roughly double that effect again; where it showed nothing, nothing followed [9]. Thinkbox's *Profit Ability 2* (2024), an econometric meta-analysis of £1.8 billion of UK media spend across 141 brands, put profit return at £1.87 per pound within 13 weeks and £4.11 over 24 months, with 58 percent of profit arriving after week 13 [10, p4, Fig 16 p41]. The same report shows why the evaluation window decides the argument: on 13 weeks, generic search returns £2.29 per pound and linear TV £1.82; on 24 months, search reaches £3.52 and linear TV £5.94 [10, Figs 10-11, p29-31].

## The challenge

Three lines of attack, and they land differently.

**Selection.** The databank is built from award entries. In 2018 Binet wrote that "these are not run-of-the-mill campaigns", that the team added cases judges had rejected as ineffective, and that even so "our sample would still be somewhat biased. All we could do was look at the differences between the good, the better and the best" [12]. *Effectiveness in Context* concedes "a biased sample of campaigns that tend to be successful" and adds that comparisons "with non-biased samples from other studies" suggest the results "are not greatly different" [5, footnote 2, p6]. The B2B report calls the bias "modest" [6]. That comparison has not been published. So: the bias is acknowledged, its size is asserted, and its effect on the ratio is unknown.

**The average.** Sixty-forty was read off how UK media spend happened to split in 2011, then found to coincide with peak efficiency in a small sub-sample [1, p37-39]. The authors' own rule is not "spend 60:40"; it is "set brand SOV equal to activation SOV or (equivalently) to match their competitors' brand/activation split" [1, p39]. The number survived because, as Sharp put it, "people wanted a number" [11].

**The Ehrenberg-Bass position.** Byron Sharp's most direct statement, at a summit in August 2022, reported by Mi3 and republished on the Institute's site: "they analysed a very weird data set, which is award submissions. If you wanted to solve this issue, you would never use that data" [11]. He also questioned the category itself: "people have no idea what activations really are" [11]. His own rules, in the same talk: brands need both, advertising builds the memory structures that make activation work, reach everybody, stay on air [11]. The root is Ehrenberg's 1974 argument that advertising is a weak force whose main job is "to reinforce feelings of satisfaction with brands already bought" [7]. That is not a rejection of the long effect. It is a rejection of the split as a spend category.

We found no peer-reviewed Ehrenberg-Bass paper testing 60:40, and no replication of the ratio on non-award data. The rebuttal came from practitioners noting that the Institute's own 95:5 heuristic rests on a thought exercise, not a dataset [13]. Fair, and it does not rescue the ratio.

Settled: advertising produces effects well beyond the campaign window, comparable to or larger than the immediate effect [9][10]; short-window metrics favour activation work and understate brand work [1, p53][4]. Not settled: whether any single ratio is optimal, whether 60:40 would emerge from a random sample of campaigns, and whether "brand" and "activation" are separable lines of spend or two effects of one exposure. Sharp's objection and Binet and Field's own "brand response" campaigns are closer than the noise suggests: both say the best work does both jobs at once [1, p9].

Keller's 1993 definition of customer-based [brand equity](/principles/brand-equity/), "the differential effect of brand knowledge on consumer response to the marketing of the brand", is the clearest statement of what the long is meant to build [8]. Aaker's 1991 framing of equity as an asset attached to a name is the same idea. Kotler and Keller treat brand investment as a long-run asset in *Marketing Management*. Cialdini's *Pre-Suasion* (2016) concerns the moment before a message lands and does not address how to divide a budget across time; we do not stretch it here.

## Where practitioners get it wrong

**Treating 60:40 as a target for their own spend.** The operational rule is share-of-voice parity with the category, not a fixed split [1, p39]. A brand in an 80:20 category that copies 60:40 is under-investing in brand, by the authors' own formula.

**Judging brand work on a six-month window.** The profit curves cross at about six months [1, p53]. A dashboard at that horizon concludes, correctly for the window and wrongly for the business, that activation wins. *Media in Focus* shows the trap: 65 percent of short-term cases reported very large activation effects against 33 percent of three-year cases; for very large share effects the figures were 3 and 38 percent [4].

The pull toward the short window shows up in what marketers say they will do. Nielsen's 2025 survey of 1,400 marketers found European respondents naming revenue growth as their top priority over brand awareness by 59 to 37 percent, while North America split almost evenly [15]; a year earlier, 70 percent of nearly 2,000 marketers told Nielsen they would prioritise performance marketing over brand building, in the same survey in which they named long-term ROI as their top KPI [16].

**Cutting brand where it matters most.** In high online-research categories (finance, cars, subscriptions) the databank optimum is 74 percent brand; actual allocation was about 55. In low-research categories the optimum was 55 and the actual 69 [5, p22]. Subscription brands put around 53 percent into brand against 63 for one-off purchase brands, when their optimum is higher [5, p35]. The authors call this the online fallacy [5, p22].

The budget lines follow the same drift. In the Spring 2026 CMO Survey of 308 US marketing leaders, brand-building budgets were expected to grow 5.9 percent over the next 12 months against 10.4 percent for digital marketing, and 70.6 percent of leaders said their answer to pressure to prove marketing's value is to focus on short-term impact over long-run gains [17, p33, p41].

**Our own observation.** For the physician platform the obvious plan was activation: a warm list, a founding offer, deadlines and reminders. We wrote it, then threw it out, because squeezing a warm list works briefly and then stops, and nothing in it grows the number of physicians who know the category exists. The rebuilt plan ran two speeds at once, category building alongside conversion. Three months later adopters were growing around 50% a month with no paid acquisition, and the base had more than doubled. Three months is three data points. It is still the closest thing we have seen to the long and the short working inside one budget.

## What to do with it

1. Estimate your category's brand:activation media split from public spend data and set your brand share of voice equal to your activation share of voice. That is the report's actual rule [1, p39]. 2. Before the budget year starts, classify every line of spend as brand or activation and record the rule. If a line cannot be classified, it counts as activation. 3. Report brand and activation effects on separate lines. A blended ROI never stands alone. 4. Set the evaluation window for brand work at 12 months minimum and hold one three-year metric: price elasticity, or market share from a source you do not control. 5. If you sell in a category people research online, or by subscription, start from a brand share above 60 and test downward. The databank optimum for those contexts is 74:26 [5]. 6. When pricing power is an objective, do not use price discounts as the activation mechanic. In the 2013 data, coupons and direct marketing reduced the chance of a pricing improvement; non-price consumer promotions increased it [1, Fig 14, p20]. 7. Once a year, buy an independent read of the long effect: a geographic holdout, or econometrics with a lag structure. If you cannot afford one, you cannot afford to argue about the ratio.

Figure: Volume arrives in months; pricing power takes years. Sales effects are almost fully present by six months; profit doubles between one year and two, and pricing effects are still climbing at three years.. Source: Binet and Field, 2013, IPA Effectiveness Databank 1980 to 2010, Figures 11 to 13, p19, n=996 cases (760 with coded duration). Redrawn by Brave New Media.. Unit: % of cases.

|---|---|---|---|
| 3 months | 23 | 4 | 0 |
| 6 months | 28 | 8 | 1.7 |
| 1 year | 33 | 9 | 1.8 |
| 2 years | 34 | 14 | 2.9 |
| 3 years+ | 36 | 15 | 3.1 |

The whole 60:40 rule rests on three bars from a small subset; the middle bar is the finding, and the footnote is the caveat.. |---|---|
